title: Effectiveness of a Generate–Verify–Repair Pipeline with Batfish for LLM‑Generated Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We report a preregistered paired experiment (cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1) that evaluated whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—shared initial LLM candidate (gpt-5-mini) + a deterministic Batfish‑style validator + at most one automated LLM repair—reduces deterministic‑verifier detected semantic/safety failures on intent→vendor‑CLI tasks. Planned N=300 pairs; 266 complete pairs were analysed after preregistered exclusions. Baseline pass-rate = 260/266 (97.744%); guarded (final GVR) pass-rate = 265/266 (99.624%). Paired difference = 0.01879699248; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625. Paired bootstrap (B=10,000, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.0037593984962406013, 0.03759398496240601]. Repair was invoked for 6 tasks; median repair iterations per task = 0. Per‑episode latency was not recorded in per‑task artifacts and therefore the preregistered latency bound (median ≤ 60 s) could not be assessed. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the observed absolute improvement is small and did not meet the preregistered α=0.05 decision rule. We provide preregistered design details, deterministic validator semantics, complete numeric outcomes, representative artifact‑grounded repair examples, contamination findings (no exact public duplicates flagged), and an evidence‑grounded discussion of limitations and implications.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being actively explored for NetOps tasks including intent→CLI translation, zero‑touch configuration synthesis, and automated maintenance workflows [1], and surveys highlight both opportunity and failure modes in these domains [2]. Stochastic LLM outputs can violate sequencing, reachability, and vendor constraints in ways that create operational risk when applied directly to device CLIs. A practical mitigation pattern is generate–verify–repair (GVR): generate a candidate, run a deterministic verifier (e.g., Batfish‑style reachability/ordering checks), and, if the verifier flags failures, attempt a bounded automated repair before escalation [3,4].

Motivated by limited preregistered evaluations that couple LLM generation, deterministic network verification, and bounded repair loops, we preregistered and executed a paired experiment to estimate the causal effect of a single permitted validator‑triggered automated repair on verifier pass‑rate when the baseline and guarded conditions share the exact same initial sampled candidate (shared_initial_candidate semantics). The shared_initial_candidate estimand isolates the effect of the validator‑triggered repair for that fixed initial sample rather than conflating it with independent re‑sampling or constrained first‑pass prompting. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived and the preregistration manifest SHA‑256 is provided for audit.
sections.related_work:
Recent works evaluate LLMs for network configuration tasks and propose benchmarks and prototypes that motivate verifier integration [1,2]. Generate–verify–repair and related generate‑and‑validate architectures have been proposed across code generation and regulated domains to obtain deterministic validation via external oracles and bounded repair loops [3]. Network verification tooling (Batfish, header‑space analyses) provides deterministic checks for reachability, ordering, and policy constraints and has been used as an oracle in prior NetOps prototypes [4]. Studies probing what LLMs need to synthesize correct router configurations emphasize sequencing and vendor‑syntax difficulties that motivate external verification [5].

Our study differs in three ways that address gaps identified in that literature: (1) it is preregistered with a formal paired estimand under shared_initial_candidate semantics, (2) it uses an archived deterministic validator as the binary oracle and records validator trace artifacts per episode, and (3) it reports exact paired counts, the preregistered McNemar test, and a paired bootstrap CI to quantify effect magnitude and uncertainty using archived seeds and resample counts.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The preregistered study cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1 (manifest SHA‑256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891) defined the primary estimand as paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Shared_initial_candidate semantics mean the exact same single sampled initial model candidate is used to produce both the baseline outcome (candidate → validator pass/fail) and the guarded outcome (candidate → validator; if validator fails, at most one automated repair call may be invoked; final validator pass/fail recorded). This design isolates the effect of the allowed validator‑triggered repair for a fixed initial sample and matches the preregistration's execution contract.

Task bank and sampling: The preregistered generator produced 300 deterministic intent→CLI pairs (150 Cisco‑like, 150 Juniper‑like) combining public NetConfEval‑style examples and synthetic generator outputs; generator id, seeds, and per‑task manifests are archived. Inclusion/exclusion and retry rules followed the preregistration: up to two automatic retries for transient provider failures; pairs with both‑arm provider failures were excluded from the primary analysis. After execution 34 both‑arm provider/infrastructure failures were excluded per the preregistered missingness plan, leaving 266 complete paired units for confirmatory analysis (analysis/missingness_summary.csv).

Model, orchestration, and sampling disclosure: The declared model in the archived execution configuration is gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json: declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"). Archived model fields include max_output_tokens = 1024, maximum_attempts_per_call = 1, provider = openai_responses, and temperature = null (unset). The null temperature and absence of an archived deterministic sampling seed imply nondeterministic sampling cannot be excluded for the recorded provider calls; this is explicitly disclosed in the preregistration and disclosure statement. Provider call accounting (deterministic_reconciliation.json) reports hosted_model_call_event_count = 306, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 272, and failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 34.

Deterministic validator and scoring: The binary oracle used by the experiment is deterministic_netops_validator_v5. For each candidate the validator performs syntactic parsing/normalization, per‑task required_sequence checks, allowed_field touch checks, and reachability/constraint validation against the deterministic synthetic topology. Episode artifacts archive validation_before and validation_after traces including parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation codes, and a normalized_configuration string. The validator's binary pass/fail outcome is used as the primary endpoint and is archived in execution/scoring/*.json.

Repair loop mechanics: Per preregistration the repair stage is invoked only if the validator fails the shared initial candidate; at most one automated LLM repair call is permitted (repair stage_count observed = 6). The repair prompt includes the validator's failure codes, the task constraints, and the normalized failing candidate; repaired outputs and repair provider traces are archived. The decision to bound repairs to one automated iteration was preregistered to mirror a constrained automated correction step prior to human escalation.

Inferential procedures and rationale for dual reporting: The primary confirmatory test was the exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary outcomes (α=0.05). To quantify effect magnitude and finite‑sample uncertainty we also preregistered a paired bootstrap percentile CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) for the paired difference. The McNemar test depends only on discordant counts and produces discrete p‑values in small discordant samples; the bootstrap CI complements McNemar by estimating the empirical paired‑difference distribution and so helps interpret practical effect size even when discrete tests are close to nominal thresholds. Both procedures were executed by the paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl includes bootstrap parameters).
sections.results:
Execution accounting and missingness: Planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2). Completed episodes = 532; failed episodes = 68. Complete pairs analysed = 266; both_missing_pairs = 34 excluded per preregistration (analysis/missingness_summary.csv). Provider call auditing: hosted_model_call_event_count = 306, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 272, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 34, cache_hit_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 272 (deterministic_reconciliation.json).

Primary paired outcomes: For the 266 complete pairs the paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 260 (both pass), n10 = 5 (guarded pass only), n01 = 0 (baseline pass only), n00 = 1 (both fail). Observed success rates: baseline = 260/266 = 0.9774436090; guarded = 265/266 = 0.9962406015. Absolute paired difference = 0.01879699248. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625 (preregistered α=0.05 decision rule: not significant). Paired bootstrap percentile CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) = [0.0037593984962406013, 0.03759398496240601] (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl contains seed and resample count). The discrete McNemar p and the bootstrap CI differ in implication because McNemar uses only discordant counts and yields discrete p‑values while the bootstrap CI summarizes resampled paired‑difference variability; both results are reported per the preregistered analysis plan.

Repair invocation and representative artifacts: The repair stage executed 6 times across 300 planned tasks (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 300, repair = 6). Median repair iterations per task = 0 (H2 median repair iterations preregistered statistic confirmed). Representative example: task-000008's shared initial candidate (execution/responses/task-000008-shared-initial.txt, sha256 = 89306095...) contained an incomplete final line "interface uplink2\n" and failed validation (parsed_command_count mismatch). The guarded final artifact (execution/responses/task-000008-guarded.txt, sha256 = d52b7616f...) contains a corrected complete sequence; its validator trace shows validation_after passing (execution/scoring/task-000008-guarded.json archives the accepted normalized_configuration and violation_count = 0). All repair prompts and provider traces for repaired episodes are archived when invoked.

Contamination and sensitivity: analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty—no exact public duplicates were flagged and thus none were excluded for contamination in the primary analysis. Sensitivity analysis treating the 34 excluded both‑arm episodes conservatively as failures (N=300) yields baseline = 260/300 = 0.866667 and guarded = 265/300 = 0.883333; discordant counts remain n10=5, n01=0 and McNemar p = 0.0625, indicating the primary inferential conclusion is robust to the preregistered conservative missingness handling.

Supplementary archived artifacts and reproducibility anchors: key archived SHA‑256 digests include execution/raw_results.jsonl (34fe154dde2a540f...), execution/model_configuration.json (916b386bd80cbffb...), and provenance/master_prompt.txt (1872df1e1805d2d9...). The paired_contingency_table.csv and condition_summary.csv are included in analysis artifacts (their SHA‑256 values are present in analysis artifact hashes). The bootstrap seed (1729) and resamples (10,000) are recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl.
sections.discussion:
Statistical interpretation: The guarded GVR pipeline produced an absolute increase of ≈1.88 percentage points in validator pass‑rate. Under the preregistered exact McNemar decision rule the improvement did not meet α=0.05 (p=0.0625). The paired bootstrap CI narrowly excludes zero, illustrating how finite‑sample discreteness of McNemar (dependence on small discordant counts) can yield a non‑rejection while a resampling CI suggests a small positive effect; reporting both provides a fuller inferential picture and aligns with the preregistered analysis plan.

Operational context and implications: The baseline single‑shot pass rate was high (~97.7%), so automated bounded repair had few failures to correct and invoked repairs rarely (6/300). For workloads with high first‑pass accuracy, a constrained automated repair stage yields limited marginal benefit; larger benefits may be observed in corpora with lower baseline accuracy, with more permissive repair budgets, or when verifier coverage increases to detect additional semantic failure classes. These implications are conditional on the validator's coverage and the specific model/version used in this experiment.

Threats to validity: Internal validity: by design, shared_initial_candidate semantics measure only the effect of validator‑triggered repair on a fixed initial candidate; our experiment does not evaluate independent re‑sampling or constrained first‑pass prompting strategies. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a finite rule set (syntactic parsing, required_sequence, allowed_field, reachability checks); semantic violations outside that battery are not detected and therefore unmeasured. External validity: the task corpus mixes public NetConfEval‑style examples and seeded synthetic tasks limited to two vendor dialect clusters; results do not automatically generalize to other vendors, larger production topologies, or different workload distributions. Conclusion validity: small discordant counts (n10=5, n01=0) and exclusion of 34 provider‑failure pairs reduced effective sample size and precision; larger N or task banks with lower baseline pass rates would yield more informative discordant counts for McNemar testing.

Design lessons and reproducibility recommendations: (1) Record per‑episode pipeline timestamps to enable preregistered latency analyses (H2 latency bound could not be evaluated here because per‑episode latency was not archived). (2) Expand validator rule batteries and document coverage to reduce construct‑validity uncertainty and enable measurement of verifier false negatives. (3) When baseline pass rates are high, design experiments either with larger N or target more challenging task subsets to increase power for detecting small absolute improvements. (4) Preserve and publish archived artifacts and manifest SHA‑256 values (as we do) so other researchers can re‑compute paired counts and reproduce bootstrap intervals from the same raw results.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired evaluation of a GVR pipeline that combined a single sampled initial LLM candidate (gpt‑5‑mini), a deterministic_netops_validator_v5 oracle, and a bounded automated repair stage (≤1 repair). Among 266 complete paired units the guarded pipeline improved verifier pass rate by 0.01879699248 but did not meet the preregistered McNemar α=0.05 decision rule (p=0.0625); a paired bootstrap CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) narrowly excludes zero. Repair calls were rare (6/300) and median repair iterations per task = 0. Per‑episode latency was not archived and therefore the preregistered latency bound could not be assessed. All execution and analysis artifacts and hash manifests are archived to support reanalysis.

References
[1] C. Wang, M. Scazzariello, A. Farshin, S. Ferlin, D. Kostić, and M. Chiesa, “NetConfEval: Can LLMs Facilitate Network Configuration?,” Proc. ACM, 2024, doi: 10.1145/3656296.
[2] S. Y. Long, J. Tan, B. Mao, F. Tang, Y. Li, M. Zhao, and N. Kato, “A Survey on Intelligent Network Operations and Performance Optimization Based on Large Language Models,” IEEE Commun. Surveys & Tutorials, 2025, doi: 10.1109/comst.2025.3526606.
[3] R. Cadenas, “Convergent Correctness in Stochastic Code Generation: A Generate‑Verify‑Repair Architecture for Deterministic Validation of Autonomous AI Coding Agents in Regulated Environments,” SSRN, 2026, doi: 10.2139/ssrn.6754899.
[4] M. Brown, A. Fogel, D. Halperin, V. Heorhiadi, R. Mahajan, and T. Millstein, “Lessons from the evolution of the Batfish configuration analysis tool,” Proc., 2023, doi: 10.1145/3603269.3604866.
[5] R. Mondal, A. Tang, R. Beckett, T. Millstein, and G. Varghese, “What do LLMs need to Synthesize Correct Router Configurations?,” Proc., 2023, doi: 10.1145/3626111.3628194.

Execution and analysis artifacts, logs, and hash manifests are archived in the evidence bundle referenced in the preregistration for audit per the track’s reproducibility requirements.
limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: both arms used the same single sampled initial candidate per preregistration; the estimand measures validator‑triggered repair benefit for that fixed initial sample and does not evaluate independent first‑pass generations or constrained first‑pass prompting strategies.

Missingness and sample reduction: planned N=300 pairs; after infrastructure/provider exclusions 266 pairs were complete and 34 both‑arm episodes were excluded per preregistered rules, reducing effective sample size and precision.
Small discordant counts: primary inference used exact McNemar with few discordants (n10=5, n01=0); conclusions are sensitive to inferential choice and limited power.
Validator coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a finite set of syntactic/semantic/reachability rules; semantic violations outside its coverage are possible and unmeasured.

Runtime nondeterminism and sampling: archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null and no deterministic seed; nondeterministic sampling cannot be excluded for recorded model calls.
H2 latency not evaluated: per‑episode end‑to‑end latency was not present in archived per‑task artifacts and therefore the preregistered latency bound (median ≤ 60 s) could not be assessed.

External validity: task corpus derives from public NetConfEval‑style examples and a seeded synthetic generator limited to two vendor‑dialect clusters; results do not imply universal benefit across other vendors, larger topologies, or production deployments.
